items.title: Morning Digest: U.S. Republicans derail bid to impeach Hegseth; Pranab Mukherjee hinted at desire to become PM, writes Sonia Gandhi in memoir, and more - The Hindu
items.excerpt: Published - November 11, 2026 06:42 am IST ... #### U.S. Republicans derail bid to impeach Hegseth Republicans in the U.S. House of Representatives on Tuesday (November 10, 2026) blocked an effort to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth over the Iran war, handing President Donald Trump a victory days after his party’s crushing midterm election defeat. The House voted 211 to 204 to send the impeachment resolution to the Judiciary Committee, effectively derailing a planned vote on Wednesday (November 11, 2026) on whether to bring formal charges against the embattled Pentagon chief. #### Pranab Mukherjee hinted at desire to become PM, ‘shocked’ me, writes Sonia Gandhi Former President Pranab Mukherjee had “shocked” Sonia Gandhi by hinting at his “long-held desire” to become Prime Minister during a conversation with her in 2010, suggesting that perhaps it was time for a “change at the top”, the former Congress president has written in her memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love. #### Supreme Court goes beyond Deepavali AQI, flags vehicular emissions polluting Delhi air Forty-eight hours before Deepavali, amidst the rising crescendo of crackers heralding the festivities, a Supreme Court Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said the people, and not the judiciary, must strike a blow against air pollution in the national capital. Instead, the court went beyond Deepavali to highlight a consistent danger that sustains and would worsen the toxic air: vehicular emissions. On November 6, the court detected a sharp increase in issues attributable to vehicular emissions. ... #### After Bangladesh rules out passport for Hasina, India says ‘travel document’ needed A day after the Acting Foreign Minister of Bangladesh, Humayun Kabir, stressed that Dhaka would not issue a passport to deposed Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and insisted on getting her extradited from India under an “acceptable prisoner exchange”, the Ministry of External Affairs said on Tuesday (November 10, 2026) that a “travel document” was needed for international travel.

items.title: CPI inflation report: October 2026
items.excerpt: Costs for goods and services rose more than expected in October, providing fresh warning signs for the Federal Reserve in its fight to lower inflation. The consumer price index, a broad gauge of costs across the U.S. economy, increased a seasonally adjusted 0.4% for the month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Tuesday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had been looking for a 0.3% increase. Stripping out volatile food and energy, so-called core CPI increased 0.3% against the forecast for a 0.2% gain. The headline CPI had increased 0.6% in September while core was up 0.3%. The report comes at a critical juncture for the Federal Reserve as it considers its next interest-rate move. Speaking Tuesday morning in London ahead of the CPI release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a hot inflation report could push him toward advocating for a half-point increase in December, and specifically said such a hike should be on the table if core CPI was "around 0.3." Hours later, that's exactly what happened. Traders are now fully pricing in a quarter percentage-point increase when the Fed next meets Dec. 8-9, and put odds of a half-point hike at 13.6%, after being around zero prior to the inflation report, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Stocks fell following the release, while Treasury yields jumped. ... The BLS did not estimate a yearly rate in its October inflation report. The government shutdown last year prevented the bureau from collecting sufficient data in October 2025, so there is no comparable figure to use. However, the report did include annual figures for some individual items where it was able to collect data. Though gasoline prices have been falling in recent weeks, the energy index rose 0.7% and the gasoline index was up 1%. The natural gas index, though, was off 0.8%. Food costs accelerated 0.5%, pushed higher by increases of 1% for snacks, 0.9% for beef and 0.5% for meats, poultry, fish and eggs. Transportation services jumped 0.8%. New vehicle prices increased 0.2% but used cars and trucks fell 1.2%. Shelter costs were higher by 0.3%, which the BLS said accounted for more than 30% of the headline increase. Apparel, a tariff-sensitive sector, rose just 0.1%. Medical care commodities prices increased 0.5%. Airline fares accelerated 0.4%. ... Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, speaking Tuesday after the inflation report, said she sees a need for two additional quarter-point increases. Logan noted that the CPI report was "higher than expected" and said she is worried that the Fed's primary inflation-forecasting metric, the personal consumption expenditures price index, also could move higher when it is reported later in November. "It may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the [Federal Open Market Committee] has moved so far this fall," she said. "After two more increases are in place, it would make sense in my view to pause and examine economic and financial developments to determine what further action may be appropriate." In addition to tariffs and the war, inflation has been pressured by hyperscaler spending in the artificial intelligence buildout. Electricity prices rose 0.9%, a potential complication from the AI story. Anna Paulson, the president of the Philadelphia Fed, listed tariffs, energy prices, and the AI buildout as the "main factors have been keeping inflation elevated," in remarks later Tuesday, though she pointed to research that said the effects from tariffs were "beginning to fade." But she said the Tuesday data suggest "inflation pressures are still very much with us." "For now, further gradual tightening seems appropriate," said Paulson in her prepared remarks. "But the exact path will depend on how conditions evolve, and I'll be watching the data closely." For now, consumers continue to spend — retail sales rose 0.8% in September, according to the Commerce Department — but businesses plan more price hikes. A net 37% of businesses responding to the October National Federation of Independent Business survey reported that they plan to raise prices in the next three months, the highest level since July 2022.

items.title: Inflation runs hotter than expected as higher prices extend beyond the gas station | PBS News
items.excerpt: Economy Nov 10, 2026 12:59 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. inflation was higher than expected last month as the rising prices that powered sweeping Democratic victories in last week's midterm elections appear likely to pose ongoing challenges for the White House and the Federal Reserve. The consumer price index rose 0.4% from September to October, the Labor Department said Tuesday, down from 0.6% the previous month. The government did not report a yearly inflation rate because last year's government shutdown meant no data was released for October 2025. But excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 0.3%, the same as the preceding month. Both figures were a tenth of a point higher than forecast, and at an annual rate would be well above the Fed's 2% target. The new inflation data heightened concerns that strong consumer and business spending, combined with higher gas prices and supply disruptions stemming from tariffs and global turmoil, are creating increasingly stubborn inflation that could extend beyond temporary spikes in prices at the gas pump. The economy expanded at a 3.4% annual rate in the July-September quarter, mostly driven by consumer spending. "It's worrisome. There is a sense that inflation is broad, persistent, a little bit everywhere," said Riccardo Trezzi, founder of Underlying Inflation, a consulting firm, and a former Fed economist. "The Fed should be very worried." Using rough estimates for last October's data, Trezzi calculates that consumer prices rose 4% in October from a year ago, up from 3.7% in September. Core prices rose 2.8%, he estimates, up from 2.6%. ... ## Federal Reserve may become more aggressive ... The persistence of elevated inflation makes it highly likely that the Fed will raise its key interest rate at its next meeting in December. It kept rates unchanged late last month, after raising them in September. The Fed increases borrowing costs in an effort to cool spending and bring down inflation. Earlier Tuesday, Fed governor Christopher Waller, an outspoken member of the central bank's rate-setting committee, said that a hike of a half-point next month was possible, double the size of the usual quarter-point increase. "Economic activity is strong, the labor market is stable, but inflation is too high, well above" the Fed's 2% goal, Waller said. Stock prices fell in early trading Tuesday, and Treasury yields rose, on expectations of more persistent inflation and higher rates from the Fed. ## Higher gas prices may have begun to spread through economy Gas prices rose 1% from September to October, the government said, a stiff increase but still much lower than in previous months. Gas prices have soared more than 37% from a year ago. Still, oil prices have fallen sharply in recent days on hopes that the Iran conflict is fading, and gas costs have declined this month. Yet there are signs higher energy prices are spreading into other parts of the economy, with air fares, public transportation, and delivery services all jumping in price. Electricity prices rose 0.9% from September to October, the most since April, and grocery prices jumped 0.4%, a painful rise after years of increases. Beef prices rose 0.9% last month, after jumping nearly 14% in the first half of this year. Restaurant prices rose 0.5% from September to October, the most since January 2024. Rising shipping prices, driven up by more expensive gas, have lifted costs for restaurants and grocery stores, which may be passing them on to consumers. Inflation has also been worsened by the massive investments flowing into artificial intelligence, which has contributed to higher prices for computer chips, electricity and consumer electronics. Voters swept dozens of candidates into office who had pledged to slow data center construction. Computer prices jumped 0.5% last month, the government report showed, after rising nearly 10% in the year ending in September, lifted by more expensive chips. The cost of computers had been retreating for years as semiconductor chips became more efficient. That trend reversed course this year as prices rose sharply. ... Prices are also rising in some sectors that have little to do with oil and gas or AI. Streaming video services have recently gotten more expensive, with Disney raising prices last month for its ad-supported Disney+ and Hulu streaming bundle to $12.49 a month from $11.99. The ad-free version rose by $2.50 to $21.49. ... Outside of inflation, other measures show the economy is largely doing well. The unemployment rate is a low 4.1% and growth is steady. Still, high prices have left most Americans with a dour view of the economy.

items.title: Fed’s Bowman says ’still work to do’ on inflation By Reuters
items.excerpt: Nov 10 (Reuters) - Federal Reserve Vice Chair of Supervision Michelle Bowman on Tuesday added her voice to the chorus of colleagues pointing to inflation as their biggest priority, though she stopped short of calling for interest-rate hikes and said she expects price pressures to abate next year as the effect of recent shocks wears off. "Today, I am seeing signs that inflation pressures are persisting, while labor market conditions appear to be firming," Bowman said in remarks prepared for delivery to the Council on Foreign Relations in Washington, DC. "This indicates that there is still work to do to bring inflation closer to 2%." The core personal consumption expenditures price index likely rose 3.3% in October, she said, driven by higher energy prices and AI-related demand. But lack of progress on inflation, she added, has not been driven by the labor market, which has improved but is not overheated. As pressures from the AI buildout and the Middle East conflict "wane or unwind and with no inflationary pressures emerging in the labor market, my forecast is for core PCE inflation to move closer to 2% next year," she said.

items.title: The Democratic leadership revolt has a glaring problem
items.excerpt: The Republican leadership fights are over. For Democrats, the pain has only just begun. Why it matters: All the talk about changing party leadership is empty if no one steps up to run. - Senate Republicans demanded more time and deeper conversations about their leadership, but no one stepped forward to challenge John Thune, who won by acclamation. - Democrats are demanding their own conversations about the party's future and the leadership of Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries. Neither has a challenger. ‼️ The intrigue: Where there was a contested leadership fight, the challenger won. - Rep. Jim Jordan, the Freedom Caucus founding member who spent years tormenting Republican leaders, will now lead the battered House GOP after defeating 12-year leadership veteran Rep. Steve Scalise by 33 votes. - Jordan is the kind of fighter House Republicans want to take on Democrats as they enter the minority, lawmakers told Axios. - "We're gearing up for war. And you're talking to a guy who's known as a hammer. You know we need someone who can punch hard, and I think that he'll do that," Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.) told Axios. 🤺 Zoom in: No such fighter has emerged to challenge Democratic leaders from within their ranks, and Schumer said he is "confident I will be elected majority leader." - The closest thing to a challenge is Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who's listening to calls to run for Democratic leader while also considering a presidential campaign. It's hard to do both. - Meanwhile, opposition to Schumer is building: " [T]he time is now for change," Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said Tuesday. He appeared with Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), who said she's not "actively seeking the job" but demanded a plan for change. 🏛️ Over in the House, Jeffries is dismissive of the idea that anyone would challenge him after the midterms gave him a massive majority. - "You think I don't have the vote nailed down? I guess we'll find out next Wednesday," he told reporters on Monday. - Some of his new members are signaling that they're not afraid to defy their new leaders. Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio) said it "aches" his heart to potentially oppose the first Black speaker, "but Rome is burning." - But other new members are on Jeffries' side, like Reps.-elect Marni von Wilpert (D-Calif.), Denise Powell (D-Neb.) and Cait Conley (D-N.Y.). 🤝 Jeffries also has high-profile progressive incumbents on board, such as Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Ro Khanna (D-Calif.). - "There is one candidate in this race, Hakeem Jeffries, and I think that everyone is far more concerned about what that leadership means, what is it promising?" Ocasio-Cortez told reporters on Tuesday.

items.title: US House blocks bid to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, for now
items.excerpt: An effort to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war on Iran without congressional authorisation, has failed on Capitol Hill. A majority of the House of Representatives agreed to refer impeachment articles to a committee - essentially killing the effort introduced by dissident Republican congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky - for now. In his first news briefing from the Pentagon in six months, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a "farce" and "sabotage". The bid to find the cabinet secretary guilty of misconduct and ultimately remove him from office was seen as a long shot as it could have required a number of other Republicans to defy President Donald Trump. Massie was the only Republican to vote against moving the resolution to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee on Tuesday. His effort failed in a 211-204 vote, with more than a dozen members, including 11 Democrats, missing the vote. The move to send the measure to the panel effectively kills the effort, as there is only a short period of time left in this Congress before Democrats take control in January. ... Impeachment resolutions can be carried past the end of a congressional term, meaning Democrats would be able to take it up next year. The Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress in January following a successful midterm election that allowed them control of both chambers. ... In the eight articles of impeachment formally introduced in the House on Monday, Massie said Hegseth was "breaking the law and must be held accountable" for fighting a war in Iran for more than 90 days without lawmakers' approval. The impeachment articles also accused Hegseth of overseeing "extrajudicial killings" in the US campaign against boats alleged to be carrying drugs in the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea.

items.title: Trump replaces judicial nominee in last-ditch bid to reshape US appeals court
items.excerpt: Nov 10 (Reuters) - The White House withdrew and replaced one of President Donald Trump's judicial nominees on Tuesday, after opposition from Republican senators cast doubt on ‌his ability to fill a key US appeals court seat before Democrats take control ‌of the Senate. The White House said Trump rescinded Arkansas-based US District Judge Lee Rudofsky's nomination to the St. Louis-based 8th US ​Circuit Court of Appeals and instead nominated Arkansas Supreme Court Justice J. Cody Hiland. The White House and Senate Republicans are racing to confirm as many new judges as possible before Democrats take control of the Senate in January after winning at least 54 seats in the November 3 midterm elections. Trump appointed ‌Rudofsky as a federal district ⁠court judge in Little Rock in 2019, and prominent conservative lawyers had supported his decision in August to try to elevate the judge to the 8th ⁠Circuit when a seat opened up. The appeals court hears cases from federal courts in Arkansas, Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota and South Dakota. If Trump secured another appointee on it, 10 of its 11 ​active ​judges would have been appointed by Republican presidents and ​6 by Trump himself. But Rudofsky's prospects dimmed ‌after the election as reports emerged that Arkansas' two Republican senators, John Boozman and Tom Cotton, favored someone else to fill the Arkansas seat on the court. Their opposition drew attention after Mike Davis, a Trump ally at conservative legal activist group Article III Project, accused them on Friday in a social media post of committing an "unforgivable sin" by jeopardizing the seat by blocking Rudofsky. Hiland, who ‌has served on Arkansas' top state court since 2023, ​said at an August event at a law school in ​Arkansas that he had expected to receive ​the appeals court nomination but was instead offered a federal district judgeship. "And ‌so, being belligerent at times, I said no," ​Hiland told the crowd, ​according to a video. "That is not a position that I'm interested in." Hiland and the senators did not respond to requests for comment. Rudofsky said in a statement that "the reality is that, ​without the support of my ‌home-state senators, confirmation is simply not a practical possibility in today's Senate."

items.title: Fight or flight? Trump mixes signals after midterms
items.excerpt: President Donald Trump's political mantra is "fight, fight, fight." But he has given decidedly mixed messages about whether he will do so after Republicans were hammered in the midterms. In the week since becoming a lame duck, Trump named the hardline architect of his migration crackdown as his chief of staff, while admitting his deportation policy was too tough. The 80-year-old raised eyebrows when he publicly asked Ultimate Fighting Championship boss Dana White to be his new press secretary -- then claimed he was just joking. He has admitted that the Iran war was largely to blame for the midterms rout. But he has strongly backed Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth's battle against impeachment. And despite saying on election night that he'd accept the results of the Democratic sweep, he has reverted to type and revived baseless claims of election fraud. "One of the characteristics of Donald Trump is that he changes his mind on a dime," Democratic Senator Chris Coons told CNN. "He'll be praising someone on Monday, firing them on Tuesday, and pretending he never knew them on Wednesday. So it's hard to predict exactly what Donald Trump is going to do." ... Democrats have promised to rein in Trump and launch a series of investigations into corruption and abuse of power. He could face a third impeachment. But for a president supposedly facing his last stand, he has at times struck a surprisingly conciliatory tone. As results came in, he congratulated Democrats on seizing Congress and said he could work with them. ... And when Trump announced on Friday that ultraloyalist Stephen Miller would replace Susie Wiles as his chief of staff, it seemed that the gloves were finally off. The brains behind the masked immigration raids that left two Americans dead, Miller has also been instrumental in using executive orders to help Trump bypass Congress. Yet in an interview the same day -- though broadcast on Sunday -- Trump conceded voters had been turned off by the aggressive deportation push. "I think it was too tough," Trump told the CBS News "60 Minutes" program. Still, the chances of Trump doing a deal with Democrats -- possibly even for an amnesty for undocumented migrants -- remain low. "It doesn't seem likely. Not with this decision to have Stephen Miller running the show," Sarah Binder, a senior fellow in governance studies at the Brookings Institution, said in a panel discussion this week.

items.excerpt: November 11, 2026 ... There’s so much music coming out all the time that it’s hard to keep track. On those days when the influx of new tracks is particularly overwhelmin g, we sift through the noise to bring you a curated list of the most interesting new releases (the best of which will be added to our Best New Songs playlist). Below, check out our track roundup for Tuesday, November 10, 2026. ### Beach Bunny – ‘Vinegar’ Beach Bunny have announced their signing to Atlantic Records with a new single called ‘Vinegar’. The vigorous, anthemic track finds frontperson Lili Trifilio taking “aim at big business,” per a press release, which is funny, especially when you factor in the Office Space/ Severance-inspired music video, directed by Hannah Klein. “‘Vinegar’ is less a discussion and more a bubbling resentment directed at the 21st century mass commodification of everything,” Trifilio commented. “The song was inspired by conversations shared with friends in soul-sucking jobs trying to make ends meet, fears around ai, and an ongoing frustration with mass consumerism, commercialization, and greed. It’s impossible to escape being observed, marketed to, and influenced, but it’s important to be aware and question if what you’re being sold is in your best interest.” ### Palehound – ‘Natural Disasters’ “My basement is flooding, and your house is burning, and we’re not talking,” Ella Kempner sings on ‘Natural Disasters’, the stirring lead single from their just-announced Palehound LP, You Sing Like You’re Joking. In a press release, they said, “I was like, ‘Damn, the future is pretty doomy right now. Why can’t we just get over it and get through this together?’” The track comes paired with a music video directed by Water From Your Eyes’ Rachel Brown. ### Sex Week – ‘Ears as an Organ of Touch’ Artist Spotlight alumni Sex Week have announced their debut LP, Ears as an Organ of Touch, which is out February 12 via Grand Jury. It includes the previously released ‘Life Is A Circle’, and the catchy, alluring title track arrives today. The album was written and recorded in the first year the pair lived together in their Brooklyn apartment. “It feels like our life,” Richard Orofino said. ### Dirty Projectors – ‘Jumbotron’ That’s David Longstreth playing the piano on ‘Jumbotron’, Dirty Projector’s first release since signing to Joyful Noise and launching their own imprint, Well Tempered Zealot. ... ### Tove Lo – ‘Blood In Your Eyes’ Tove Lo’s ‘Blood in Your Eyes’ is the latest preview of the star-studded Grand Theft Auto VI soundtrack. The bouncy track is also featured on a new GTA 6 promo video announcing that pre-loads are now live. ### King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard – ‘Rogue Wave’ King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard’s rave era continues with Entropy, a companion album to their 2026 LP Alien Metal.
